newsitem.title: USA: Report shows bond firm gifts to Ill. officials.
newsitem.headline: Report shows bond firm gifts to Ill. officials.

text.p: Several securities and bond counsel firms spent money on state of Illinois officials in 1996, according to a report released Tuesday by a government watchdog group.

Citizen Action reported that officials with the Illinois Housing Development Authority, Illinois Student Assistance Commission, Illinois Development Finance Authority and members of Gov. Jim Edgar's staff received gifts from firms involved in the municipal bond business.

The report was based on 1996 expenditure filings required under the state's Lobbyist Registration Act made by firms and individuals lobbying for state contracts by a Jan. 30 deadline, according to John Cameron, an associate director of Citizen Action.
The spending levels by muni firms were about the lowest since the law was passed in 1993.
LaSalle National Bank spent $142.50 taking Bobby Wilkerson, director of the Illinois Development Finance Authority to a Chicago Bulls basketball game, according to the report.
Alex. Brown & Sons also spent $30.23 on Wilkerson, while Principal Financial Services spent $55.57 on Richard Frampton, a program administrator at the agency.

PaineWebber Inc. spent a total of $70.22 on Josh Hershman, general counsel of the student assistance commission, while Larry Matejka, its executive director, was the beneficiary of $62 of spending from Bear, Stearns & Co. and $95.48 from Chapman and Cutler, according to the report.
The report showed Everen Securities spent $26.99 on Andy Foster, Edgar's deputy chief of staff, while Smith Barney, Inc. spent $77.13 on Edgar's assistant press secretary Gary Mack.
Bell Boyd & Lloyd spent a total of $84.66 on two officials at the housing authority, while Stifel Nicolaus & Co. spent $10 on one official, the report indicated.
Citizen Action released the report, which also detailed spending by other businesses and groups involved in state matters, to push for a bill that would impose an outright ban on such gifts.

"Big-time lobbyists are buying after-hours access to the state officials whose decisions will benefit their clients," said State Rep. Jan Schakowsky, D-Evanston, the chief sponsor of the bill, in a news release. "It's inappropriate and time to stop."
The proposed state gift ban act would make it illegal for state constitutional officers, lawmakers and appointed officials to accept gifts from lobbyists.
The bill, which has attracted a dozen sponsors, is pending before a House committee, Cameron said.
